screens.title: When Mom asks again
screens.body: The same question, five times before dinner. It’s one of the most common changes families notice, and one of the most tiring. In about 9 minutes you’ll learn why it happens and what to say instead.
bullets: Why the question keeps coming back
What to avoid, even when it’s true
Practice out loud, then make a plan

screens.title: Where do Mom's repeated questions usually reach you?
screens.body: Your answer changes the examples and your task, not the lesson.

screens.title: What would you say?
screens.setup: You’re at work. Mom calls for the third time today:
screens.line: When are you coming on Saturday?
screens.note: Just your first instinct. There’s no wrong answer yet; we’ll come back to this.

answers.text: Saturday morning, around ten. Write it down so you remember.
Mom, I told you already. Saturday. I’m at work.
You’re wondering when I’ll come. I’ll call you before I leave, so you don’t have to keep track. What are you doing right now?

screens.title: New information doesn’t stick
body: Memory changes make it hard to hold on to something new, like a time or a plan. Older memories often last much longer.
So the answer you gave ten minutes ago may simply be gone. To her, the question is new.
screens.keyIdea: It’s not that Mom isn’t listening. The answer didn’t stay.

screens.title: The feeling stays, even when the memory fades
body: Here’s the part most people don’t know: even when the memory of a conversation is gone, the feeling it left can stay.
If the last answer felt rushed or annoyed, Mom may not remember why, but may still feel uneasy. If it felt calm, that calm can stay too.
screens.keyIdea: How you answer matters as much as what you answer.

screens.title: Mom asks again five minutes after you answered. What’s most likely going on?

options.text: Mom is testing your patience.
Mom didn’t hear you the first time.
The answer faded, but the worry behind the question didn’t.

screens.title: What’s often behind the question
body: The words are about a time or a plan. The need underneath is usually something else:

items.title: Worry
items.text: Something is coming up and she can’t keep track of it.

items.title: Feeling lost in time
items.text: Without a clear sense of the day, plans feel shaky.

items.title: Boredom
items.text: With nothing to do, the same thought loops.

items.title: Wanting you close
items.text: The question is a way to connect.

screens.title: Mom has been sitting alone all afternoon and keeps asking when dinner is. What might help most?

options.text: Tell her the exact time again, a bit louder.
Give her something to do with you, like setting the table.
Ignore it until the questions stop.

screens.title: One pattern for the question that keeps coming back
body: Instead of repeating the facts, answer in three short steps:

steps.title: Reassure
steps.text: “We have plenty of time. I’ll tell you when.”

steps.title: Offer something to do
steps.text: “Want to help me with the tea?”

screens.keyIdea: You’ll use this same pattern in every lesson of this module.

screens.title: Step 1: Notice the feeling
body: Put the feeling into words before anything else. It tells her you’re on Mom's side.
screens.tip: “Don’t worry” sounds kind, but it can tell her the feeling is wrong. Naming it works better.

screens.title: Which reply notices the feeling?

options.text: “Don’t worry, it’s all fine.”
“You’re not sure what’s happening tomorrow, are you?”
“The appointment is at 2 pm on Thursday.”

screens.title: Step 2: Reassure
body: Take the job of remembering off her. Short, calm and the same each time.
Promise only what you’ll really do, like telling her when it’s time.

examples.text: We have plenty of time. I’ll tell you when.
examples.why: Takes the job of remembering off her

examples.text: I’ve got it covered. You don’t have to keep track.

screens.title: Step 3: Offer something to do
body: A worried loop is hard to stop with words alone. Busy hands help.
Pick something small and familiar, ideally something Mom enjoys.

items.title: Tea together
items.text: Make it, pour it, sit down

items.title: A short walk
items.text: To the garden or the mailbox

screens.keyIdea: You’re not distracting her from the truth. You’re helping the worry settle.

screens.title: Build a reply in three steps
screens.body: Pick one part for each step. Then read your reply out loud.

options.text: You’re wondering about tomorrow.
I already told you.
Don’t worry.
Like I said, it’s at 2.
We have plenty of time. I’ll tell you when.
Stop asking, it’s fine.
Want to help me with the tea?
Go watch TV.
Let’s talk about it later.

screens.title: Phrases that hurt, even when they’re true
body: After the fifth time, these come out on their own. Each one points at the forgetting, so the worry grows instead of settling.
screens.tip: If one slips out, it’s okay. Take a breath and start again with the feeling.

screens.title: Explaining the whole plan in detail helps her remember it.

options.text: True
False

screens.title: Make the answer easy to find
body: Ask her to keep a note by the phone with your next visit: “Saturday. I’ll call before I leave.”
On calls you can say: “Check the note by the phone. I’ll call before I leave.”
screens.keyIdea: And mention plans closer to the time: less waiting means less worrying.
screens.tip: In a care home, ask the staff to keep your visit days on a calendar in Mom's room.

screens.title: Mom has a dentist visit next Friday. When is a good time to tell her?

options.text: Today, so Mom has plenty of notice.
The morning of the visit, with a note on the fridge.
Don’t tell her at all.

screens.title: Look for a pattern
body: Notice when the questions come. Is it the same time of day? After a nap? When Mom is hungry, tired or has nothing to do?
If you spot a pattern, you can get ahead of it: tea at 4, a walk before dinner.
screens.tip: If repeated questions are new or suddenly much worse, mention it at the next doctor visit.

screens.title: The fifth time is the hardest
screens.body: Feeling frustrated is normal. It doesn’t mean you care any less. A small reset before you answer makes a big difference.
screens.question: Pick your reset for next time:

options.label: One slow breath before I answer
Step away for a minute, if it’s safe

screens.title: Mom asks for the fourth time when a visitor is coming. Which reply follows all three steps?

options.text: “Someone’s coming Sunday. I told you this morning.”
“You’re looking forward to the visit. It’s Sunday. Want to set out the good cups?”
“Don’t worry, everything’s fine.”

screens.title: New skill: handling repeated questions
learned: The answer fades, but the feeling stays.
Answer the feeling first: notice, reassure, offer something to do.
Skip “I told you already”. Short and the same each time.
Make the answer easy to find, and mention plans closer to the time.
